Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 40, verses 1–3:

(p-141) Surat Ghafir

Meccan according to al-Hasan, ʿAta', ʿIkrimah and Jabir. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: except for two verses of it, which were revealed in Medina, and they are ﴿Indeed, those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ [Ghafir: 56] and the one that follows it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Ha Mim﴾. Regarding it there are five interpretations:

First: It is one of the names of Allah, by which He swears. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: It is one of the names of the Qur'an. This was said by Qatadah.

Third: They are disjoined letters from the name of Allah, which is al-Rahman. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: "Ra", "Ha", "Mim" and "Nun" make up "al-Rahman."

Fourth: It is Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad.

Fifth: It is the opening letters of the surahs. This was said by Mujahid. Shurayh ibn Awfa al-ʿAbsi said:

"It reminds me of Ha Mim while the spear is thrusting; would that he had recited Ha Mim before the advance."

It may also bear a sixth meaning: that its sense is "hamma amru Allah," i.e., the command of Allah has drawn near. The poet said:

"My day has drawn near, so a people rejoiced, a people heedless and asleep."

From this comes the name of fever (al-hummah), because it brings death near.

Based on this, it may have two meanings:

First: that it refers to the nearness of the Hour, in accordance with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I was sent in its final part, a thousand..."

Second: that it refers to the nearness of His support for His allies and His vengeance upon His enemies on the Day of Badr.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Forgiver of sin﴾. Regarding it there are three interpretations:

First: He forgives it for whoever seeks His forgiveness. This was said by al-Naqqash.

Second: He conceals it for whomever He wills. This was said by Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah.

﴿Accepter of repentance﴾: it may be the plural of tawbah (repentance), and it may be a verbal noun from taba, yatubu, tawban. His acceptance of repentance is the removal of sin through it together with the bestowal of reward upon it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Owner of bounty﴾. Regarding it there are six interpretations:

First: Owner of blessings. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: Owner of power. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Third: Owner of wealth and abundance. This was said by Mujahid.

Fourth: Owner of goodness. This was said by Zayd ibn al-Asamm.

Fifth: Owner of favor (al-mann). This was said by ʿIkrimah.

Sixth: Owner of superiority (al-tafdil). This was said by Muhammad ibn Kaʿb.

The difference between al-mann and al-fadl is that al-mann is pardon for a sin, while al-fadl is a kindness not owed. Al-tawl is derived from al-tul (length), as if it is His bestowal upon others; it was also said that it is because the duration of His bestowal is long.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 40, verses 4–6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations:

One: they do not argue about them (yumari, "to dispute, to quarrel"). This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: they deny them (yajhadu). This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

Regarding the difference between mujadala (contentious disputation) and munazara (debate, examination of a question together), there are two views:

One: mujadala occurs only between two parties who are both in error, or between one who is in error and one who is right, whereas munazara occurs between two parties who are both right.

The second: mujadala is turning a person away from his position, whether he is right or wrong, whereas munazara is reaching the truth from either side, whichever it may be.

It has been said that he meant by this al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi, who was one of the mockers.

﴿So let not their movement through the land deceive you﴾. Qatada said: their coming and going, and their movement in their journeys. Regarding it there are two interpretations:

One: let not their movement through the world without punishment deceive you. This was said by Yahya.

The second: let not their movement in ease and blessing deceive you. This was said by Muqatil. It has been said that the Muslims said, "We are in hardship while the disbelievers are in ease," and so this was revealed: ﴿So let not their movement through the land deceive you﴾. This was related by al-Naqqash, and there is an ellipsis in it, its estimated meaning being: "So let not their movement through the land deceive you while they are safe; for they will surely be seized."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And every nation plotted against their messenger to seize him﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations:

One: to imprison him and torment him. This was related by Ibn Qutayba.

The second: to kill him. This was said by Qatada and al-Suddi.

The Arabs say: al-asir al-akhidh, because he is a captive for killing (al-akhidh, "the one seized"). Qutrub recited the verse of the poet:

"If you seize me, you will kill me; and whoever is seized, there is no eternity for him."

Regarding the time of their seizing their messenger there are two views:

One: at the time of his supplication against them.

The second: at the time of the descent of punishment upon them.

﴿And they disputed with falsehood in order to refute by it the truth﴾. Yahya ibn Salam said: they disputed with the prophets by means of associating partners with God, in order to nullify faith by it.

﴿So I seized them﴾. al-Suddi said: so I punished them.

﴿So how was My punishment?﴾ Regarding this question there are two interpretations:

One: that it is a question about the truth of the punishment. Muqatil said: they found it to be true.

The second: about its description. Qatada said: "By God, it was severe."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus the word of your Lord has come true against those who disbelieved﴾, meaning: just as it came true against those, it came true against these.

Regarding its interpretation there are two interpretations:

One: thus the punishment of your Lord became due.

The second: thus the promise of your Lord was fulfilled.

﴿That they are the companions of the Fire﴾. He made them its companions because they are bound to it and it is bound to them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 40, verse 10–14:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve will be called out to⦆ — there are two interpretations regarding this:

One: that they will be called out on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: they will be called out in the Fire. This was said by al-Suddi.

﴿The hatred of Allah towards you is greater than your hatred of yourselves, when you were being called to faith and you disbelieved⦆ — there are two interpretations regarding this:

One: the hatred of Allah towards you in the world, when you were called to faith and you disbelieved, is greater than your hatred of yourselves in the Hereafter, when you witnessed the punishment and knew that you were among the people of the Fire. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: its meaning is: Allah's hatred towards you, when you disobeyed Him, is greater than the hatred some of you have for one another, when you knew that they had led you astray. This was related by Ibn 'Isa.

If it is asked: how is it valid, according to the first interpretation, that they hate themselves? There are two answers:

One: they made themselves deserving of hatred through their sins.

The second: when they reached a state in which their desires departed from them and they knew that it was their own souls that had brought them to ruin through disobedience, they hated them.

Regarding the lam in ﴿Indeed, the hatred of Allah⦆ there are two interpretations:

One: it is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'), as in the saying "Zayd is indeed better than 'Amr." This was said by the Basran grammarians.

The second: it is the lam of oath, which enters upon a narration and what resembles it. This was said by Tha'lab.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, You have made us die twice and You have given us life twice⦆ — there are three interpretations regarding this:

One: He created them dead in the loins of their fathers, then gave them life by bringing them out, then caused them to die when their terms ended, then gave them life for the Resurrection. Thus there are two deaths: one in the loins of men, and the second in the world; and two lives: one in the world and the second in the Hereafter. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Qatadah.

The second: that Allah gave them life when He took the covenant from them in the back of Adam, by His saying ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their backs, their descendants⦆ [al-A'raf: 172], and so on.

Then Allah caused them to die after taking the covenant from them, then gave them life when He brought them out, then caused them to die when their terms ended, then gave them life for the Resurrection. So there are two lives and two deaths in the world and one life in the Hereafter. This was said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.

The third: that Allah gave them life when He created them in the world, then caused them to die in it when their terms ended, then gave them life in their graves for questioning, then caused them to die until the time of resurrection.

Then He gave them life for the Resurrection. This was said by al-Suddi.

﴿So we acknowledge our sins⦆ — they denied the resurrection in the world and that they would be given life after death; then in the Hereafter they acknowledged two lives after two deaths.

﴿Is there any way out?⦆ — there are two interpretations regarding this:

One: is there a path by which we may return to the world, so that we affirm the resurrection? This is the meaning of Qatadah's saying.

The second: is there a deed by which we may leave the Fire and be freed from the punishment? This was said by al-Hasan.

In the speech there is an implied element, whose estimate is: there is no way to exit.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿That is because, when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved⦆ — meaning: you disbelieved in the Oneness of Allah.

﴿But when partners were associated with Him, you believed⦆ — there are two interpretations regarding this:

One: its meaning is that you would affirm those who associated partners with Him. This was said by al-Naqqash.

The second: you would believe in idols. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

﴿So the judgment belongs to Allah⦆ — meaning: in the requiting of the disbelievers and the punishment of the disobedient.

﴿the Most High, the Most Great⦆ — it is permissible to describe Him as ʿAliyy (Most High) but it is not permissible to describe Him as Rafi' (Exalted), because the former is a quality that may be transferred from loftiness of place to loftiness of rank, whereas rafi' is used only for elevation of place.

First: He raised the seven heavens. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Kalbi.

Second: He is great in attributes. This was said by Ibn Ziyad.

Third: It means His raising the degrees of His friends (awliya'). This was said by Yahya.

﴿Lord of the Throne﴾. There are two aspects to this:

One: that His Throne is above His heavens. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Second: that He is the Lord of the Throne. This was said by Yahya.

﴿He sends down the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾. There are six interpretations of this:

First: that the Spirit is the revelation. This was said by Qatadah.

Second: prophethood. This was said by al-Suddi.

Third: the Qur'an. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Fourth: mercy. This was related by Ibrahim al-Jawni.

Fifth: the spirits of His servants; no angel descends except that there is with him a spirit from them. This was said by Mujahid.

Sixth: Gabriel, whom Allah sends by His command. This was said by al-Dahhak.

One: that Allah warns through it of the Day of Resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan.

Second: that His prophets warn of the Day of Meeting, which is the Day of Resurrection. In this there are three aspects:

First: because on it the people of the heavens and the people of the earth meet. This was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd.

Second: because on it the first and the last meet. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: on it the created and the Creator meet. This was said by Qatadah.

One: that He brings them forth all together, because nothing of them is hidden from Allah.

Second: its meaning is that He recompenses them, and nothing of their deeds is hidden from Him.

One: that it is His saying between the two blasts, when the creatures have perished and only the Creator remains, so He sees no owner or owned other than Himself: "Whose is the dominion today?" Second: that all the creatures, believers and disbelievers, answer Him, and they say: To Allah, the One, the Subduer. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun*) on Surah 40, verses 18–20:

His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying: ﴿And warn them of the Imminent Day﴾. Concerning it there are two views:

The first: it is the day of the arrival of death (al-manīyah). This was said by Qutrub.

The second: it is the Day of Resurrection. It is called "the Imminent" (al-Āzifah) because of its nearness, and every imminent thing is near. From this is His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿The Imminent has drawn near﴾ [al-Najm: 57], meaning the Resurrection has drawn near.

﴿When the hearts are at the throats﴾. Concerning it there are two views:

The first: the hearts are the souls, which have reached the throats at the arrival of death. This is the view of those who interpreted "the Imminent Day" as the arrival of death, and it was said by Qatadah.

And they stood at the throats from fear, so they neither leave nor return to their places.

﴿Choking with grief﴾ (kāẓimīn). Concerning it there are four meanings:

The first: grieved (maghmūmūn). Said by al-Kalbi.

The second: weeping (bākūn). Said by Ibn Jurayj.

The third: holding their throats (mumsikūn bi-ḥanājirihim), derived from kazm al-qirbah (kazm), which is tying the mouth of the waterskin.

The fourth: silent (sākitūn). Said by Qutrub, who recited the verse of al-Shammākh:

"So she remained, as if the birds above her heads were fasting, keeping the sun at bay while they were silent (kaẓūm)."

Ibn 'Isa said: al-kāẓim is the one who is silent while being full of rage.

﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend nor any intercessor who is obeyed﴾. Concerning ḥamīm (intimate friend) there are two views:

The first: that it is the close relative. Said by al-Hasan.

The second: that it is the compassionate friend. Said by Mujahid. The meaning of the statement is: they will have no intimate friend who benefits them, nor any intercessor who is obeyed, that is, whose intercession is granted. The granting is called obedience (ṭā'ah) because it accords with the will of the one whose request is granted.

His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾. Concerning it there are five meanings: (p-150) The first: it is signaling with the eye. Said by al-Suddi.

The second: it is a glance after a glance. Said by Sufyan.

The third: the stealthy glance. Said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: looking at what has been forbidden. Said by Mujahid.

The fifth: it is a person's saying, "I did not see," when he has seen, or "I saw," when he did not see. Said by al-Dahhak.

Concerning calling it "the treachery of the eyes" there are two explanations:

The first: because it is the most hidden of signals, so through concealment it becomes like betrayal.

The second: because stealing a glance at what is forbidden is a betrayal.

﴿And what the breasts conceal﴾. Concerning it there are three interpretations:

The first: the whisperings (al-waswasah). Said by al-Suddi.

The second: what one harbors when one sees a woman, if one were able over her, whether one would commit fornication with her or not. Said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 40, verses 23–27:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And Pharaoh said, "Leave me to kill Moses"﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

First: its meaning is, "Advise me concerning the killing of Moses," because they had advised him not to kill him, since if he killed him they would prevent him. This was said by Ibn Ziyad.

Second: "Leave me to take charge of killing him," because they had said that Moses is a sorcerer, and if you kill him you will be destroyed, for if he ordered his killing they would oppose him.

Third: that among his people there were believers who would prevent him from killing him.

So he asked them to enable him to kill him.

﴿And let him call upon his Lord﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

One of them: "And let him ask his Lord, for he will not be answered."

The second: "And let him seek help from Him, for he will not be helped."

﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

One of them: he will change your affair in which you are, said by Qatadah.

The second: its meaning is that he will act in obedience to God; narrated by Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah.

The third: his fighting Pharaoh with those who believe in him; related by Ibn 'Isa.

The fourth: that they will kill your sons and spare your women if they overcome you, as you used to do to them; said by Ibn Jurayj.

And it may be a fifth: that your dominion will end because of him, for no religion has ever emerged without a dominion ending through it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 40, verses 28–29:

His saying, may He be exalted and mighty: ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said﴾. Regarding him there are two views:

One: that he was a cousin of Pharaoh. This is related by al-Suddi, who said: "He is the one who was saved along with Musa."

The second: that he was a Copt of Pharaoh's kind, but not of his family. This is related by Muqatil.

Ibn Ishaq said: His name was Habib.

al-Kalbi related that his name was Hizbil, and that he was a king over half the people, and he had the kingship after Pharaoh, in the position of the heir apparent.

Ibn Abbas said: No one from the family of Pharaoh was a believer besides him and Pharaoh's wife, and the non-believer who gave warning, when he said, ﴿Indeed, the chiefs are conspiring against you﴾ [al-Qasas: 20].

Regarding his faith there are two views:

One: that he believed upon the coming of Musa and his confirmation of him, and this is the apparent meaning.

The second: that he was a believer before the coming of Musa, and likewise Pharaoh's wife. This is related by al-Hasan. Thus he concealed his faith. al-Dahhak said: He was concealing his faith out of gentleness toward his people, then he revealed it and said that statement while he was still concealing it.

(p-153) ﴿Would you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah"﴾, i.e., because of his saying "My Lord is Allah."

﴿And he has certainly come to you with clear evidences from your Lord﴾. Regarding these there are two views:

One: that they are the lawful and the unlawful, related by al-Suddi.

The second: that they are the signs that came to them: his hand, his staff, the flood, and others, as He, exalted, said: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of fruits﴾ [al-A'raf: 130]. This is related by Yahya.

﴿And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie﴾. This was not out of any doubt on his part regarding his message and truthfulness, but rather a gentle way of seeking to restrain them and to draw them away from harm.

﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will strike you﴾. Regarding this there are four aspects:

First: that he had promised them salvation if they believed and destruction if they disbelieved, so he said ﴿some of what he promises you will strike you﴾, because when they are in one of the two states, one of the two matters will reach them, and so that becomes part of the promise, not all of it.

The second: because he had threatened them, for their disbelief, with destruction in this world and punishment in the Hereafter, so their destruction in this world became part of what he had promised them.

The third: that what first befalls them of punishment is its beginning, then it follows them state after state until it is completed. So what strikes them is part of what he promised them, because he warned them of what they doubted, which is the first state, and what follows it they would be certain of.

The fourth: that "part" is sometimes used in the place of "all," as a gentle form of address and a broadening of speech, as the poet said:

"The deliberate one may attain some of his need, and the hasty one may also meet with error."

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar﴾. This may bear two meanings:

One: "a transgressor against himself, a liar against his Lord," pointing to Musa, and in this case it is part of the believer's speech.

The second: "a transgressor in his obstinacy, a liar in his claim," pointing to Pharaoh, and in this case it is part of the speech of Him, exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted and mighty: ﴿O my people, for you is the kingdom today, dominant in the land﴾. al-Suddi said: Victorious over the land of Egypt, prevailing over its people. This is the statement of the believer, reminding them of the blessings of Allah upon them.

﴿So who will support us against the might of Allah if it comes to us?﴾ i.e., against the punishment of Allah, warning them of retribution. He reminded and warned, so Pharaoh knew that his love (for them) had become manifest.

﴿Pharaoh said, "I only show you what I see"﴾. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: its meaning is, "I only advise you with what I see for myself."

﴿And I only guide you to the path of right conduct﴾ — in denying Musa and in believing in me.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 40, verses 30–35:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling Out (al-tanad)﴾. He means the Day of Resurrection. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

؎ And He scattered creation within it when He spread it out; they are its inhabitants until the Calling Out.

It is called that because some of them call out to one another. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Regarding what they call out to one another, there are two opinions:

The first: "Alas for our regret! Woe to us! O our destruction!" This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

The second: the people of Paradise call out to the people of the Fire, "Indeed we have found true what our Lord promised us," [Al-A'raf: 44] to the end of the verse.

(p-155) And the people of the Fire call out to the people of Paradise, ﴿Pour upon us some water, or some of what Allah has provided you﴾ [Al-A'raf: 50]. This is the view of Qatadah.

Al-Kalbi used to read it as "Yawm al-tannadd" (with a shaddah), meaning the Day of Fleeing. He said: they will flee (yannidduna) as a camel bolts (yannidd).

It has been reported in a hadith that "people will have a rush (jawlah) on the Day of Resurrection, fleeing (yannidduna), seeking to find a refuge." Then he recited this verse.

﴿The day you turn back, retreating﴾. There are two interpretations of this:

The first: retreating in their rush toward the Fire. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: retreating in their flight from the Fire, until they are hurled into it. This is the view of al-Suddi.

﴿You will have no protector from Allah. Whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾. Regarding this, there are two interpretations:

The first: "no helper." This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: "no preventer." The root meaning of ʿisma is prevention. This is the view of Ibn ʿIsa.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And Joseph certainly came to you before with clear proofs﴾. Regarding this, there are two opinions:

The first: Joseph son of Jacob, whom Allah sent as a messenger to the Copts (al-Qibt) after the death of the king before Moses, with clear proofs. Ibn Jurayj said: these were the dreams.

The second: what al-Naqqash related from al-Dahhak, that Allah sent to them a messenger from the jinn named Yusuf.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 40, verse 41–50:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Laa jaram﴾ (certainly, without doubt) has three meanings:

First: its meaning is: "there is no escaping it" (la budda), said by al-Mufaddal.

Second: its meaning is: "indeed it is right and it has been made certain" (laqad haqqa wa-istahaqqa), said by al-Mubarrad.

Third: that it is only used as a response, like the saying of one who says: "They did such-and-such," and the one answering says: "Laa jaram that they will regret," said by al-Khalil.

﴿Inna-ma tad'unanee ilayhi﴾ means: from worshipping what you worship besides Allah.

﴿Laysa lahu da'watun fid-dunyaa wa laa fil-aakhirah﴾ (has no call in this world or in the Hereafter). Regarding this there are three opinions:

First: it does not answer anyone in this world or in the Hereafter, said by al-Suddi.

Second: it neither benefits nor harms in this world or in the Hereafter, said by Qatadah.

Third: it has no intercession in this world or in the Hereafter, said by al-Kalbi.

﴿Wa anna marradanaa ilaa Allah﴾ (and that our return is to Allah) means: our return after death is to Allah, so that He may recompense us for our deeds.

﴿Wa anna al-musrifeena hum ashaab al-naar﴾ (and that the transgressors are the companions of the Fire). Regarding them there are two opinions:

First: it means the polytheists, said by Qatadah.

Second: it means those who shed blood unjustly, said by al-Sha'bi. Mujahid said: Allah called killing "israf" (excess).

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Fasa-tadhkuroona maa aqoolu lakum﴾ (so you will remember what I say to you). Regarding this there are two opinions:

First: it means in the Hereafter, said by Ibn Zayd.

Second: at the descent of punishment upon them, said by al-Naqqash.

﴿Wa ufawwidu amree ilaa Allah﴾ (and I entrust my affair to Allah). Regarding this there are three meanings:

First: its meaning is: "and I submit my affair to Allah," said by Ibn 'Eesa.

Second: "I call Allah to witness against you," said by Ibn Bahr.

Third: "I rely upon Allah," said by Yahya ibn Salam.

﴿Inna Allaha baseerun bil-'ibaad﴾ (indeed Allah is seeing of His servants). Regarding this there are two meanings:

First: with the deeds of the servants.

Second: with the final destination of the servants.

Concerning the speaker of this, there are two opinions:

First: that it is the saying of Musa.

Second: that it is the saying of the believer from the family of Pharaoh; according to this, by this statement he makes his faith manifest.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Fawaqahu Allahu sayyi'aati maa makaroo﴾ (so Allah protected him from the evil of what they plotted). Regarding this there are two opinions:

First: that Allah protected Musa from the evil of what they plotted. According to this there are two opinions:

First: that Allah saved the believer of the family of Pharaoh together with Musa until he crossed the sea, and Allah drowned Pharaoh, said by Qatadah. It was also said that "the family of Pharaoh" refers to Pharaoh alone, and from this is the saying of Araka al-Thaqafi:

"Do not weep for a dead one after the death of beloveds: 'Ali, 'Abbas, and the family of Abu Bakr."

He means Abu Bakr.

Second: that the believer of the family of Pharaoh went out from his presence fleeing to a mountain in which he prayed. Pharaoh sent for him, and the messengers came while he was in prayer, and wild beasts and animals had been repelling them from reaching him. So they returned to Pharaoh and informed him, and he killed them. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Fawaqahu Allahu sayyi'aati maa makaroo﴾.

﴿Wa haaqa bi-aali Fir'awna soo'u al-'adhaab﴾ (and the evil punishment encompassed the family of Pharaoh). Regarding this there are two meanings:

First: that they are his people, and the evil punishment is drowning, said by al-Dahhak.

Second: his messengers whom he killed, and the evil punishment is killing.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Al-Naaru yu'radoona 'alayhaa ghuduwwan wa 'ashiyyan﴾ (the Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening). Regarding this there are three opinions:

First: that their seats from the Fire are presented to them morning and evening, and it is said to the family of Pharaoh, as rebuke: "These are your abodes," said by Qatadah.

Second: that their spirits are in the bellies of black birds that go out toward Hell in the morning and return in the evening, and that is their being exposed to it, said by Ibn Mas'ud.

Third: that they are punished with the Fire in their graves morning and evening, and this is specific to the family of Pharaoh.

Mujahid said: "as long as the world lasts."

﴿Wa yawma taqoomu al-saa'ah﴾ (and the Day the Hour is established). Its establishment is the existence of its attributes in a fixed manner, and from it comes "qiyam al-suq" (the market being established), which is the presence of its people in a fixed manner at the customary time.

﴿Adkhiloo aala Fir'awna ashadda al-'adhaab﴾ (Enter the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment), because the punishment of Hell is varied.

Al-Farra' regarded the sentence as having inversion and displacement, its meaning being: "Enter the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment, the Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening," and this is contrary to what others have held, that the sentence stands in its natural order.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on Surah 40, verses 51–56:**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, We surely help Our messengers and those who believe, in the life of this world﴾. There are two views concerning it:

The first: [It means] by making their proof prevail. This was said by Abu al-Aliyah.

The second: [It means] by taking vengeance on their enemies. al-Suddi said: "No people ever killed a prophet, or a group of the believing callers to the truth, except that Allah sent someone to avenge them, and so they become victorious in this world even if they were killed."

﴿And on the day when the witnesses stand up﴾, meaning the Day of Resurrection.

Concerning their being helped, there are two views:

The first: [It means] by raising their word and multiplying their reward.

The second: [It means] that it is by taking vengeance on their enemies.

Concerning ﴿the witnesses﴾, there are three sayings:

The first: they are the angels, who testified for the prophets that they conveyed [the message], and against the nations that they denied [it]. This was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The second: they are the angels and the prophets. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: they are four: the angels, the prophets, the believers, and the body parts. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam. Furthermore, concerning ﴿al-ashhad﴾ there are also two possibilities:

The first: it is the plural of shahid, like sharif and ashraf.

The second: it is the plural of shahid in the sense of shahid, like sahib and as-hab.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾. There are two views concerning it:

The first: it is what Allah promised His Messenger in two verses of the Qur'an, that He would punish the disbelievers of Makkah. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: it is what Allah promised His Messenger, that He would give it to the believers in the Hereafter. This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

﴿And seek forgiveness for your sin﴾, meaning, for a sin if it was from you.

al-Fudayl said: "The interpretation of seeking forgiveness is: 'Release me [from it]'."

﴿And exalt the praise of your Lord﴾. Mujahid said: "And pray by the command of your Lord."

﴿In the evening and the morning﴾. There are three sayings concerning it:

The first: they are the Asr prayer and the Fajr prayer. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: al-'ashiyy is the declining of the sun until it sets, and al-ibkar is the beginning of dawn. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: they are the prayers of Makkah before the five prayers were made obligatory: two rak'ahs in the morning and two rak'ahs in the evening. This was said by al-Hasan.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without authority having come to them﴾, meaning, without a proof having come to them.

﴿There is nothing in their breasts except pride, which they will never attain﴾. There are two views concerning it:

The first: that the pride is the greatness that the disbelievers of Quraysh [possessed], which they will never attain. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it is what is exalted in belief. Concerning it there are two views:

The first: it is what the disbelievers of Quraysh hoped regarding the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, that he and they would perish. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: the Jews said that the Dajjal is one of us, and they magnified his matter, believing that they would rule and take vengeance. This was said by Abu al-Aliyah.

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of what they say, ﴿the All-Seeing﴾ of what they conceal.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations:

The third: It is greater than the deeds of mankind, when He humbled the disbelievers by force and kept them far away by subjugation.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 40, verse 60:

First: its meaning is, "Affirm My lordship [tawhid al-rububiyyah], and I will forgive you your sins." This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: "Worship Me, and I will respond to you," said by Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah, meaning: "I will accept you in your worship."

Third: "Ask Me, and I will give to you," said by al-Suddi.

The response to the one who calls upon Him, when the desire is sincere, is restricted by the condition of wisdom (hikmah).

Qatadah related that Ka'b said: "This community has been given three things which no community before you has been given, except a prophet. When a prophet was sent, it was said to him, 'You are a witness over your community,' whereas [Allah said of this community], ﴿and made you witnesses over mankind﴾. It was said to the Prophet, ﴿There is no hardship upon you in the religion﴾, whereas He said to this community, ﴿and He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾. It was said to the Prophet, 'Call upon Me, and I will respond to you,' whereas He said to this community, ﴿Call upon Me; I will respond to you.﴾"

One: that you may rest therein from the labor of the day.

The third: that you may take account of yourselves therein for what you did during the day.

In joy and exultation there are two interpretations:

First: "joy" (al-farah) is happiness, and "exultation" (al-maraḥ) is insolence (al-baṭar). So they rejoiced in being given respite and became insolent through the blessings.

Second: "joy" (al-farah) is delight and happiness, as said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and "exultation" (al-maraḥ) is transgression.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 40, verses 82–85:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿So when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they rejoiced in what knowledge they had.﴾ Regarding this there are four interpretations:

First: by their saying, "We are more knowledgeable than them; we will not be resurrected, we will not be punished." This was said by Mujahid.

Second: by what they had, which they considered to be knowledge while it was ignorance. This was said by al-Suddi.

Third: the messengers rejoiced in the knowledge they had of their own deliverance and the destruction of their enemies. This was related by Ibn ʿIsa.

(p-166) Fourth: they were content with their knowledge and mocked their messengers. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿And there descended upon them﴾ regarding this there are two interpretations:

One: it surrounded them. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Second: it returned upon them.

﴿That which they used to mock﴾ regarding this there are two interpretations:

One: Muhammad (ﷺ), that he is a sorcerer.

Second: the Qur'an, that it is poetry.
